title: Egyptian temples and the Christian faith
source_text: Παραβάλλειν δὲ τὰ τῆς πίστεως ἡμῶν τοῖς Αἰγυπτίων θέλει πράγμασι· παρ᾿ οἷς προσιόντι μέν ἐστι λαμπρὰ τεμένη καὶ ἄλση καὶ προπυλαίων μεγέθη τε καὶ κάλλη καὶ νεῲ θαυμάσιοι καὶ σκηναὶ πέριξ ὑπερήφανοι καὶ θρησκεῖαι μάλα δεισιδαίμονες καὶ μυστηριώτιδες, ἤδη δὲ εἰσιόντι καὶ ἐνδοτέρω γινομένῳ θεωρεῖται προσκυνούμενος αἴλουρος ἢ πίθηκος ἢ κροκόδειλος ἢ τράγος ἢ κύων. τί γὰρ τὸ ἀνάλογον τοῖς πρὸς τοὺς προσιόντας σεμνοφανέσιν Αἰγυπτίων ἐστὶ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν, τί δὲ τὸ ἀνάλογον τοῖς ἔνδον μετὰ τὰ σεμνὰ προπύλαια ἀλόγοις ζῴοις προσκυνουμένοις; ἢ τὰς μὲν προφητείας καὶ τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν καὶ τὰ κατὰ τῶν ἀγαλμάτων †ἐστὶ τὰ καὶ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν σεμνὰ, Ἰησοῦς δὲ Χριστὸς ἐσταυρωμένος τὸ ἀνάλογον τῷ προσκυνουμένῳ ἀλόγῳ ζῴῳ; ἀλλ᾿ ἐὰν τοῦτο λέγῃ (οὐ γὰρ ἄλλο τι οἶμαι φήσειν αὐτὸν), ἀπαντήσομεν ὅτι πλείονα ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ἡμῖν εἰς κατασκευὴν τῶν κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν εἴρηται, ὅτι καὶ τὰ δοκοῦντα κατ᾿ ἄνθρωπον αὐτῷ συμβεβηκέναι χρησίμως γέγονεν [ἐν] τῷ παντὶ καὶ σωτηρίως τῷ ὅλῳ κόσμῳ.
pass_a_gloss: He wishes (θέλει) to compare (παραβάλλειν) the things of our faith (πίστις) with the affairs (πράγματα) of the Egyptians; among whom for one approaching (προσιών) there are splendid precincts (λαμπρὰ τεμένη) and groves (ἄλση) and sizes and beauties of gateways (προπύλαια) and wonderful temples (νεῲ θαυμάσιοι) and tents (σκηναί) round about, magnificent (ὑπερήφανοι), and rites (θρησκεῖαι) very superstitious (δεισιδαίμονες) and mystery-like (μυστηριώτιδες); but for one already entering and getting further inside (ἐνδοτέρω) there is beheld (θεωρεῖται) being worshipped a cat (αἴλουρος) or ape (πίθηκος) or crocodile (κροκόδειλος) or goat (τράγος) or dog (κύων). For what is the counterpart (τὸ ἀνάλογον) among us to the solemn-looking things (σεμνοφανῆ) of the Egyptians toward those approaching, and what the counterpart to the irrational animals (ἄλογα ζῷα) worshipped inside after the solemn gateways? Or are the prophecies (προφητεῖαι) and the God over all and the things against the images [crux] the solemn things also according to him, but Jesus Christ crucified (ἐσταυρωμένος) the counterpart of the worshipped irrational animal? But if he says this (for I think he will say nothing else), we shall answer (ἀπαντήσομεν) that more has been said by us in the things above for the establishing (κατασκευή) of the things about Jesus, that even the things seeming to have happened to him as a man (κατ᾿ ἄνθρωπον) have come about usefully (χρησίμως) for the whole (τῷ παντί) and savingly (σωτηρίως) for the whole world (ὅλος κόσμος).
pass_b_english: He wants to compare the things of our faith with the practices of the Egyptians. Among them, as one approaches, there are splendid sacred precincts and groves, great and beautiful gateways, wonderful temples, magnificent pavilions all around, and rites deeply devout and full of mystery; but once one has gone in and further inside, what one sees being worshipped is a cat, or an ape, or a crocodile, or a goat, or a dog.

What, then, is there among us that corresponds to the things of the Egyptians that look solemn to those approaching, and what corresponds to the irrational animals worshipped inside, beyond the solemn gateways? Or are the prophecies, the God over all, and the teaching against images the things that even he counts solemn, while Jesus Christ crucified corresponds to the irrational animal that is worshipped? If he says this (and I do not think he will say anything else), we will answer that a good deal has already been said by us above in support of what concerns Jesus: that even what seems to have befallen him as a man has come about for the good of the universe and for the salvation of the whole world.

choices.choice: The description of the Egyptian temples is Origen's report of Celsus's comparison, framed as indirect report ('he wants to compare ... among whom'), so it is not put in quotation marks; it probably follows Celsus's own wording closely. Crux: the staged text marks †ἐστὶ τὰ καὶ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν σεμνά as corrupt; rendered on the sense 'are the prophecies, the God over all and the teaching against images the things that even in his view are solemn', taking τὰ κατὰ τῶν ἀγαλμάτων as the Christian teaching against idols. The bracketed [ἐν] before τῷ παντί is treated as deleted by the editor. τῷ παντί rendered 'the universe' (the whole of things), distinct from τῷ ὅλῳ κόσμῳ 'the whole world'. 'Above' (ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω) refers back to the earlier books on the passion. No Scripture quoted; the phrase 'the whole world' is not tied to a single verse and is left uncited. 'Jesus Christ crucified' may echo 1 Corinthians 2:2 or 1:23, but here it is Origen's guess at Celsus's comparison, so it is a possible allusion only and not cited inline. δεισιδαίμονες rendered 'deeply devout' (not 'superstitious'), since the clause lists what looks impressive from outside; τὰ δοκοῦντα (present) rendered 'what seems', and kept clear of any docetic sense.
